regulation_query: lawful bases for processing personal data, GDPR
cited_chunk_ids: gdpr-en-article-6-1-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-6-2-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-6-3-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-6-4-2016-05-04
answer: The GDPR lists six lawful bases for processing personal data in Article 6(1): (a) the data subject has given consent for one or more specific purposes; (b) processing is necessary for the performance of a contract to which the data subject is a party or to take steps at the data subject’s request before entering into a contract; (c) processing is necessary for compliance with a legal obligation to which the controller is subject; (d) processing is necessary to protect the vital interests of the data subject or another natural person; (e) processing is necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority vested in the controller; (f) processing is necessary for the purposes of the legitimate interests pursued by the controller or a third party, unless overridden by the data subject’s interests or fundamental rights (this basis does not apply to public authorities when performing their tasks) [1].

regulation_query: personal data breach notification deadline supervisory authority GDPR
cited_chunk_ids: gdpr-en-article-33-1-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-33-2-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-33-3-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-33-4-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-33-5-2016-05-04
answer: A personal data breach must be reported to the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, no later than 72 hours after the controller becomes aware of it [1].

regulation_query: GDPR data breach notification obligation, timing of informing data subjects, Article 33 and 34 requirements, breach to affected individuals
cited_chunk_ids: gdpr-de-article-34-1-2016-05-04 gdpr-de-article-34-2-2016-05-04 gdpr-de-article-34-3-2016-05-04 gdpr-de-article-34-4-2016-05-04
answer: Eine Datenpanne muss den betroffenen Personen unverzüglich mitgeteilt werden, wenn die Verletzung des Schutzes personenbezogener Daten voraussichtlich ein hohes Risiko für die persönlichen Rechte und Freiheiten natürlicher Personen zur Folge hat [1]. Die Benachrichtigung muss in klarer und einfacher Sprache erfolgen und die in Art. 33 Abs. 3 Buchstaben b‑d genannten Informationen enthalten. Ist jedoch einer der in Art. 34 Abs. 3 genannten Ausnahmen erfüllt – zum Beispiel weil geeignete technische und organisatorische Sicherheitsvorkehrungen (wie Verschlüsselung) angewendet wurden, weil nachträgliche Maßnahmen das hohe Risiko praktisch beseitigt haben oder weil die Benachrichtigung mit einem unverhältnismäßigen Aufwand verbunden wäre – ist die direkte Benachrichtigung der betroffenen Personen nicht erforderlich; stattdessen kann eine öffentliche Bekanntmachung oder eine vergleichbare Maßnahme erfolgen [1].

regulation_query: designation of data protection officer, GDPR, obligation for controllers and processors, criteria for appointment
cited_chunk_ids: gdpr-en-article-37-1-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-37-2-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-37-3-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-37-4-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-37-5-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-37-6-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-37-7-2016-05-04
answer: A controller or processor must appoint a data protection officer when any of the following applies: (a) the processing is carried out by a public authority or body (except courts acting in their judicial capacity); (b) the core activities consist of processing that, by its nature, scope or purposes, involves regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale; or (c) the core activities consist of processing on a large scale of special categories of data under Article 9 or personal data concerning criminal convictions or offences under Article 10 [1]. A group of undertakings may designate a single DPO if the officer is easily accessible from each establishment, and where the controller or processor is a public authority, a single DPO may be designated for several such authorities or bodies, taking account of their organisational structure and size [1]. In cases not covered by these three criteria, a DPO may still be required if Union or Member State law mandates it [1].

regulation_query: maximum administrative fine GDPR
cited_chunk_ids: gdpr-en-article-83-1-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-83-2-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-83-3-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-83-4-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-83-5-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-83-6-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-83-7-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-83-9-2016-05-04
answer: Under the GDPR, administrative fines can be up to €20 million or up to 4 % of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher. For less serious infringements the limit is €10 million or 2 % of turnover, but the overall maximum is the €20 million/4 % level [1].

regulation_query: mandatory data protection impact assessment, GDPR, circumstances requiring DPIA, processing likely to result in high risk to data subjects
cited_chunk_ids: gdpr-en-article-35-1-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-35-2-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-35-3-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-35-4-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-35-5-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-35-6-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-35-7-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-35-8-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-35-9-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-35-10-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-35-11-2016-05-04
answer: A data protection impact assessment (DPIA) is mandatory before any processing that is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, taking into account the nature, scope, context and purposes of the processing [1]. In particular, the GDPR lists three categories of processing for which a DPIA is required: (a) a systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects of individuals based on automated processing, including profiling, that leads to decisions producing legal effects or that significantly affect the individual; (b) processing on a large scale of special categories of data under Article 9(1) or of data concerning criminal convictions and offences under Article 10; and (c) systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area on a large scale [1]. Additionally, the supervisory authority may publish lists of processing operations that must or need not undergo a DPIA, and those lists are communicated to the relevant bodies [1].

regulation_query: GDPR record of processing activities exemption for controllers with fewer than 250 employees
cited_chunk_ids: gdpr-en-article-30-1-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-30-2-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-30-3-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-30-4-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-30-5-2016-05-04
answer: The GDPR does not automatically require enterprises with fewer than 250 employees to keep a record of processing activities. Article 30(5) states that the record‑keeping obligations do not apply to such enterprises unless the processing is likely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects, the processing is not occasional, or it involves special categories of data or criminal‑offence data [1].

regulation_query: automated individual decision-making, right to object, GDPR data subject rights, AI Act high‑risk AI system, legal basis for processing
cited_chunk_ids: gdpr-en-article-22-1-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-22-2-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-22-3-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-22-4-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-21-1-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-21-5-2016-05-04
answer: Yes. Under GDPR Art. 22 a data subject has the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, that produces legal effects or similarly significant effects [1]. In addition, GDPR Art. 21 gives the data subject a right to object to processing – including profiling – on grounds relating to his or her particular situation, and the controller must stop processing unless it can demonstrate compelling legitimate grounds [5]. The objection may even be exercised by automated means where appropriate [4].

regulation_query: controller and processor contract requirements, GDPR, data processing agreement obligations, responsibilities, lawful processing, security measures, sub‑processing, data subject rights
cited_chunk_ids: gdpr-en-article-28-1-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-28-2-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-28-3-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-28-4-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-28-5-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-28-6-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-28-7-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-28-9-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-28-10-2016-05-04
answer: A contract (or other legal act) between a controller and a processor must be in writing (including electronic form) and set out the subject‑matter and duration of the processing, the nature and purpose of the processing, the type of personal data and categories of data subjects, and the obligations and rights of the controller. It must also stipulate that the processor: (a) processes the personal data only on documented instructions from the controller (including transfers to third countries unless required by law); (b) ensures that persons authorised to process the data are bound by confidentiality; (c) takes all measures required under Article 32; (d) respects the conditions for engaging another processor; (e) assists the controller, where possible, with appropriate technical and organisational measures to fulfil the controller’s obligation to respond to data‑subject rights requests; (f) assists the controller in ensuring compliance with Articles 32‑36, taking into account the nature of the processing and the information available to the processor; (g) at the controller’s choice, deletes or returns all personal data after the service ends and deletes existing copies unless storage is required by law; and (h) makes available to the controller all information necessary to demonstrate compliance and to allow audits or inspections by the controller or an auditor mandated by the controller. The processor must also immediately inform the controller if, in its opinion, an instruction infringes the GDPR. [1]

regulation_query: definition of AI system under the AI Act
cited_chunk_ids: aia-en-article-3-0-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-3-0-2026-07-27-p2 aia-en-article-3-0-2026-07-27-p3

regulation_query: verbotene KI-Praktiken nach der KI-Verordnung, unzulässige KI-Anwendungen, Echtzeit-Fernbiometrische Identifizierung, subliminale Techniken, manipulative Systeme, soziale Bewertung, Hochrisiko‑KI, AI Act
cited_chunk_ids: aia-de-article-5-1-2026-07-27 aia-de-article-5-1-2026-07-27-p2 aia-de-article-5-1a-2026-07-27 aia-de-article-5-4-2026-07-27 aia-de-article-5-6-2026-07-27 aia-de-article-5-7-2026-07-27 aia-de-article-5-8-2026-07-27
answer:
Nach Art. 5 der KI‑Verordnung (AIA) sind folgende Praktiken verboten:

- Das Inverkehrbringen, die Inbetriebnahme oder die Verwendung eines KI‑Systems, das Techniken der unterschwelligen Beeinflussung außerhalb des Bewusstseins einer Person oder absichtlich manipulative bzw. täuschende Techniken einsetzt, um das Verhalten einer Person wesentlich zu verändern und ihr dabei erheblichen Schaden zuzufügen oder mit hinreichender Wahrscheinlichkeit zuzufügen. [1]
- Das Inverkehrbringen, die Inbetriebnahme oder die Verwendung eines KI‑Systems, das eine Vulnerabilität oder Schutzbedürftigkeit einer natürlichen Person oder einer bestimmten Gruppe (z. B. wegen Alter, Behinderung oder sozialer/ökonomischer Situation) ausnutzt, um das Verhalten dieser Person wesentlich zu verändern und ihr dabei erheblichen Schaden zuzufügen oder mit hinreichender Wahrscheinlichkeit zuzufügen. [1]
- Das Inverkehrbringen, die Inbetriebnahme oder die Verwendung eines KI‑Systems, das realistische Bild‑, Video‑, Ton‑ oder ähnliche Inhalte erzeugt oder manipuliert, in denen intime Körperteile einer bestimmbaren natürlichen Person dargestellt werden oder eine eindeutig sexuelle Handlung gezeigt wird, ohne dass die betroffene Person eine freiwillige, spezifische, aufgeklärte, eindeutige und ausdrückliche Zustimmung erteilt hat. [1]
- Das Inverkehrbringen, die Inbetriebnahme oder die Verwendung eines KI‑Systems, das Material oder Darbietungen im Sinne von Art. 2 Buchstaben c und e der Richtlinie 2011/93/EU erzeugt oder manipuliert, es sei denn, nach nationalem Recht gilt das „unrechtmäßige“ Verhalten als gerechtfertigt. [1]
- Das Inverkehrbringen, die Inbetriebnahme oder die Verwendung von KI‑Systemen zur Bewertung oder Einstufung natürlicher Personen oder Gruppen über einen bestimmten Zeitraum auf Grundlage ihres sozialen Verhaltens oder bekannter, abgeleiteter oder vorhergesagter persönlicher Eigenschaften, wobei die soziale Bewertung zu einer Schlechterstellung oder Benachteiligung führt, die entweder nicht im Zusammenhang mit den ursprünglichen Daten steht oder im Hinblick auf das soziale Verhalten unverhältnismäßig ist. [1]
- Das Inverkehrbringen, die Inbetriebnahme oder die Verwendung eines KI‑Systems zur Durchführung von Risikobewertungen in Bezug auf natürliche Personen, um das Risiko, dass eine natürliche Person eine Straftat begeht, ausschließlich auf Grundlage von Profiling zu bestimmen. [1]

regulation_query: AI system used in the operation of the electricity grid, high‑risk classification, AI Act, safety component, critical infrastructure, supply of electricity
cited_chunk_ids: aia-en-article-6-1-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-1a-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-1b-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-1c-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-2-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-3-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-4-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-5-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-6-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-7-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-8-2026-07-27 aia-en-annex-iii-0-2026-07-27

regulation_query: AI system providing customer service, transparency obligations, AI Act, GDPR transparency requirements, personal data processing, information to data subjects
cited_chunk_ids: aia-en-article-50-1-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-50-2-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-50-3-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-50-4-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-50-5-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-50-6-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-50-7-2026-07-27
answer: For a customer‑service chatbot the AI Act imposes several transparency duties.  The provider must ensure that the natural persons who interact with the chatbot are informed that they are dealing with an AI system, unless this is obvious to a reasonably well‑informed, observant and circumspect user given the context (Art. 50(1)) [1].  The information must be presented in a clear and distinguishable way, at the latest at the moment of the first interaction or exposure, and must meet applicable accessibility requirements (Art. 50(5)) [1].  If the chatbot generates synthetic text (or other media) the provider must also ensure that the output is marked in a machine‑readable format and is detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, unless an exemption applies (e.g., the output is subject to human editorial control or the use is authorised for law‑enforcement purposes) (Art. 50(2)) [1].  These obligations are without prejudice to any other transparency requirements set out in Union or national law (Art. 50(6)) [1].

regulation_query: Obligations of deployers of high-risk AI systems, AI Act, compliance duties, risk management, conformity assessment, monitoring, transparency, post-market monitoring
answer:
Deployers of high‑risk AI systems must:
- Take appropriate technical and organisational measures to use the system in accordance with its instructions for use [1].
- Assign human oversight to natural persons who have the necessary competence, training, authority and support [1].
- Respect other Union or national obligations and retain freedom to organise resources for implementing the oversight measures [1].
- Ensure that any input data they control is relevant and sufficiently representative for the intended purpose of the system [1].
- Monitor the operation of the system according to the instructions, inform the provider (and, where relevant, the distributor and market‑surveillance authority) of any risk of non‑compliance, suspend use if necessary, and immediately report serious incidents to the provider, importer/distributor and authorities [1].
- Keep automatically generated logs under their control for a period appropriate to the system’s purpose, of at least six months unless other Union or national law provides otherwise [1].
- Inform workers’ representatives and affected workers before the system is put into service or used at the workplace, in line with Union and national rules on worker information [1].
- If they are public authorities or EU bodies, comply with registration obligations, refrain from using unregistered systems and inform the provider or distributor [1].
- Use the information provided under Article 13 of the AI Regulation to carry out a data‑protection impact assessment under the GDPR (Art. 35) or the relevant data‑protection directive [1].
- For post‑remote biometric identification, request authorisation ex ante or within 48 hours from a judicial authority and inform the relevant market‑surveillance and data‑protection authorities [1].
- Inform natural persons when the system makes or assists in decisions that affect them [1].
- Cooperate with competent authorities in any actions they take concerning the high‑risk AI system [1].

regulation_query: obligation to conduct a data protection impact assessment (fundamental rights impact assessment) under GDPR, responsible party (controller, processor) and relevant legal concepts
cited_chunk_ids: aia-en-article-27-1-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-27-2-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-27-3-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-27-4-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-27-5-2026-07-27
answer: The fundamental‑rights impact assessment must be carried out by the deployer of the high‑risk AI system.  In particular, bodies governed by public law, private entities that provide public services, and deployers of high‑risk AI systems listed in points 5(b) and 5(c) of Annex III are required to perform the assessment before the system’s first use [1].

regulation_query: AI literacy obligation requirements under the AI Act, duties of providers and users, transparency and information provision
cited_chunk_ids: aia-en-article-4-1-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-4-2-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-4-3-2026-07-27 omnibus_ai-en-article-1-0-2026-07-24 omnibus_ai-en-article-1-0-2026-07-24-p2 omnibus_ai-en-article-1-0-2026-07-24-p3
answer: The AI literacy obligation requires providers and deployers of AI systems to take measures that support the development of AI literacy among their staff and any other persons who deal with the operation and use of the AI systems on their behalf. These measures must consider the persons' technical knowledge, experience, education and training, the context in which the AI systems are used, and the persons or groups on whom the systems are intended to be used. The obligation does not require guaranteeing any specific level of AI literacy for any individual. In addition, the Commission and the Member States must support and facilitate these efforts – especially for SMEs – by publishing practical examples of how to comply on the single information platform referred to in Article 62(3), point (b). The Board must adopt recommendations, taking into account European competence frameworks, to help the Commission and Member States promote AI literacy, including setting common objectives. [1][3]

regulation_query: entities subject to DORA, digital operational resilience, financial sector, regulated entities, financial institutions, market participants
cited_chunk_ids: dora-en-article-2-1-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-2-2-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-2-3-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-2-4-2022-12-27
answer:
DORA applies to the entities listed in Article 2(1), namely: (a) credit institutions; (b) payment institutions, including those exempted under Directive (EU) 2015/2366; (c) account information service providers; (d) electronic money institutions, including those exempted under Directive 2009/110/EC; (e) investment firms; (f) crypto‑asset service providers authorised under the Regulation on markets in crypto‑assets and issuers of asset‑referenced tokens; (g) central securities depositories; (h) central counterparties; (i) trading venues; (j) trade repositories; (k) managers of alternative investment funds; (l) management companies; (m) data reporting service providers; (n) insurance and reinsurance undertakings; (o) insurance intermediaries, reinsurance intermediaries and ancillary insurance intermediaries; (p) institutions for occupational retirement provision; (q) credit rating agencies; (r) administrators of critical benchmarks; (s) crowdfunding service providers; (t) securitisation repositories; and (u) ICT third‑party service providers [1].

Paragraph 3 of the same article lists entities that are excluded, such as managers of alternative investment funds under Directive 2011/61/EU, certain insurance/reinsurance undertakings, small occupational retirement institutions, natural or legal persons exempted under Directive 2014/65/EU, micro‑enterprise insurance intermediaries, and post‑office giro institutions. Additionally, Member States may exclude further entities under paragraph 4 [1].

regulation_query: major ICT-related incident reporting obligations, deadlines, DORA incident notification requirements, reporting to competent authorities, timelines for submission
cited_chunk_ids: dora-en-article-19-1-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-19-3-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-19-4-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-19-5-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-19-6-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-19-8-2022-12-27
answer: For a major ICT‑related incident a financial entity must submit three reports to the competent authority: (a) an initial notification; (b) an intermediate report as soon as the incident’s status changes significantly or the handling changes based on new information (and thereafter whenever a relevant status update is available or on request); and (c) a final report when the root‑cause analysis is completed and the actual impact figures are known [2]. The exact time limits for the initial notification and each subsequent report are to be set by the regulatory technical standards developed under Art. 20, point (ii); those specific deadlines are not detailed in the current provisions [2].

answer: Finanzunternehmen, die nicht zu den in Art. 16 Abs. 1 Unterabs. 1 genannten Unternehmen oder Kleinstunternehmen gehören, müssen erweiterte, bedrohungsorientierte Penetrationstests (TLPT) mindestens alle drei Jahre durchführen. regulation_query: ICT third-party arrangements register, information obligations, DORA, digital operational resilience, reporting requirements
cited_chunk_ids: dora-en-article-28-1-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-28-2-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-28-3-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-28-4-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-28-5-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-28-6-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-28-7-2022-12-27
answer: Under DORA, the register of information on ICT third‑party arrangements is a record that financial entities must keep and regularly update at the entity level as well as at sub‑consolidated and consolidated levels. It contains information on all contractual arrangements with ICT third‑party service providers, distinguishing those that support critical or important functions from those that do not. The register must be documented appropriately and is used for yearly reporting to competent authorities on new arrangements, provider categories, contract types and the ICT services and functions provided. Financial entities must also make the full register or specified sections available to the competent authority on request. [1]

regulation_query: ICT outsourcing contract for critical functions, contractual obligations under GDPR for data processor and controller, DORA requirements for critical entities and ICT service providers, AI Act obligations if AI systems are involved, risk management, security and incident reporting clauses
cited_chunk_ids: dora-en-article-30-1-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-30-2-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-30-3-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-30-3-2022-12-27-p2
answer:
A DORA‑compliant ICT outsourcing contract for services that support critical or important functions must be documented in a single written agreement (paper or durable electronic format) and include the following provisions:

- A clear, complete description of all functions and ICT services to be provided, stating whether subcontracting is permitted and, if so, the conditions for such subcontracting. [3]
- The locations (regions or countries) where the contracted or subcontracted functions and data processing/storage will take place, together with a requirement for the provider to notify the financial entity in advance of any change of location. [3]
- Provisions on availability, authenticity, integrity and confidentiality of data, including personal data. [3]
- Provisions ensuring access, recovery and return of personal and non‑personal data in an easily accessible format in the event of the provider’s insolvency, resolution, discontinuation of business operations or termination of the contract. [3]
- Service‑level descriptions, including updates and revisions. [3]
- An obligation for the provider to assist the financial entity at no additional cost (or at a cost determined ex‑ante) when an ICT incident related to the provided service occurs. [3]
- An obligation for the provider to fully cooperate with competent authorities and resolution authorities of the financial entity (including any persons appointed by them). [3]
- Termination rights and minimum notice periods that meet the expectations of competent and resolution authorities. [3]
- Conditions for the provider’s participation in the financial entity’s ICT security awareness programmes and digital operational resilience training. [3]

For contracts covering critical or important functions, DORA adds further mandatory elements:

- Full service‑level descriptions with precise quantitative and qualitative performance targets to enable effective monitoring and corrective action. [3]
- Notice periods and reporting obligations, including notification of any development that could materially impact the provider’s ability to meet the agreed service levels. [3]
- Requirements for the provider to implement and test business contingency plans and to maintain ICT security measures, tools and policies appropriate to the regulatory framework. [3]
- An obligation to participate in and fully cooperate with the financial entity’s TLPT (testing, learning and penetration testing) as referred to in Articles 26 and 27. [3]
- The right of the financial entity to monitor the provider’s performance on an ongoing basis, which includes unrestricted access, inspection and audit rights, the ability to take copies of critical documentation, the possibility to agree on alternative assurance levels, and detailed provisions on the scope, procedures and frequency of such inspections and audits. [3]
- Exit‑strategy provisions, including a mandatory transition period during which the provider continues the service to reduce disruption and enables the financial entity to migrate to another provider or an in‑house solution. [3]

regulation_query: personal data breach reporting obligations under GDPR, cybersecurity incident reporting obligations under DORA, supervisory authority notification, data subject notification, risk to rights and freedoms
cited_chunk_ids: gdpr-en-article-33-1-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-33-2-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-33-3-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-33-4-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-33-5-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-34-1-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-34-2-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-34-3-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-34-4-2016-05-04 dora-en-article-19-1-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-19-2-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-19-3-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-19-4-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-19-5-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-19-6-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-19-7-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-19-8-2022-12-27
answer:
Under the GDPR, the bank (as data controller) must notify the competent supervisory authority "without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware" of the breach. The notification must include at least: a description of the nature of the breach, the categories and approximate number of data subjects and records concerned, the contact details of the data protection officer, the likely consequences of the breach, and the measures taken or proposed to address it [2]. If the breach is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of the data subjects, the bank must also communicate the breach to the affected customers in clear, plain language, providing the same information as required for the supervisory‑authority notification, unless an exemption applies (e.g., effective encryption) [3].

Under DORA, the ransomware attack qualifies as a "major ICT‑related incident" that must be reported to the relevant competent authority. The bank must submit an initial notification using the template referred to in Article 20, followed by an intermediate report whenever the status of the incident changes significantly, and a final report once the root‑cause analysis is completed and actual impact figures are available [1]. These reports must contain all information necessary for the authority to determine the significance of the incident and assess possible cross‑border impacts. The reports must be submitted within the time limits laid down in Article 20, paragraph 4(a)(ii) [1]. The bank may outsource the reporting to a third‑party provider, but remains fully responsible for fulfilling the reporting obligations [1].

regulation_query: AI system for credit scoring of consumers, high-risk classification, AI Act, personal data processing, GDPR obligations, data subject rights, transparency and accountability
cited_chunk_ids: aia-en-article-50-1-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-50-2-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-50-3-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-50-4-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-50-5-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-50-6-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-50-7-2026-07-27 gdpr-en-article-35-1-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-5-1-2016-05-04 aia-en-article-53-1-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-53-2-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-53-3-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-53-4-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-53-5-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-53-6-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-53-7-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-25-4-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-4a-1-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-55-1-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-55-2-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-55-3-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-54-6-2026-07-27
answer:
For a bank that intends to use an AI model to carry out consumer credit‑scoring, the following EU‑law obligations are triggered:

1. **Transparency to data subjects** – The bank (as deployer) must inform the natural persons that they are interacting with an AI system and must provide the required information in a clear and distinguishable way at the latest at the first interaction (Art. 50(1) AIA) [2]. If the model generates any synthetic content (e.g. synthetic text or images) the output must be marked in a machine‑readable format that makes the artificial nature detectable (Art. 50(2)) [2].

2. **Data‑protection impact assessment** – Because credit‑scoring is a new technology that is likely to entail a high risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects, the bank must carry out a DPIA before processing personal data (Art. 35(1) GDPR) [6].

3. **Compliance with GDPR principles** – The processing must respect the GDPR data‑protection principles of lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, data‑minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation and integrity/confidentiality (Art. 5(1) GDPR) [9].

4. **Contractual information from the model provider** – The bank must obtain from the provider the technical documentation, training‑ and testing‑process information and any other data needed to understand the model’s capabilities and limitations (Art. 53(1)(a)–(b) AIA) [1]. The provider must keep this documentation up‑to‑date and make it available to the bank. The bank should also include in its contract with the provider the information, capabilities and assistance required to enable the bank to meet its own obligations (Art. 25(4) AIA) [8].

5. **Bias‑detection and special‑category data** – If the credit‑scoring model processes special‑category data for bias detection, the bank may only do so when strictly necessary and must apply the safeguards listed in Art. 4a(1) AIA (e.g. pseudonymisation, limited access, deletion after bias correction) [10].

6. **Cybersecurity and systemic‑risk obligations (if applicable)** – If the AI model is classified as a general‑purpose model with systemic risk, the provider must perform adversarial testing, report serious incidents and ensure adequate cybersecurity (Art. 55(1) AIA) [3]. While these are provider duties, the bank must verify that the provider complies, for example by requiring evidence of such measures in the contractual terms.

7. **Open‑source exception** – If the AI model is released under a free and open‑source licence that makes the model parameters publicly available, the provider’s obligations under Art. 53 and Art. 54(6) do not apply, unless the model presents systemic risks. The bank’s deployer obligations (transparency, DPIA, GDPR compliance) still apply regardless of the licence [1][5].

In summary, the bank must (i) provide transparent information to consumers, (ii) conduct a DPIA, (iii) respect GDPR data‑protection principles, (iv) obtain and keep up‑to‑date technical documentation from the provider, (v) ensure contractual terms that enable compliance, (vi) apply appropriate safeguards when processing special‑category data for bias detection, and (vii) verify that any systemic‑risk obligations of the provider are met.

regulation_query: Geltungsbereich der DSGVO bei KI-Systemen, die unter die KI-Verordnung fallen, Überschneidung der Rechtsvorschriften, Anwendung personenbezogener Daten, KI-Verordnung, Datenschutzrecht
cited_chunk_ids: gdpr-de-article-2-1-2016-05-04 gdpr-de-article-2-2-2016-05-04 gdpr-de-article-2-3-2016-05-04 gdpr-de-article-2-4-2016-05-04
answer: Ja, die DSGVO bleibt weiterhin anwendbar, wenn ein KI‑System unter die KI‑Verordnung fällt. Die DSGVO gilt für jede ganz oder teilweise automatisierte Verarbeitung personenbezogener Daten, unabhängig davon, ob das System zugleich den Anforderungen der KI‑Verordnung unterliegt [2]. Da die KI‑Verordnung keine ausdrückliche Ausnahme von der DSGVO enthält, bleibt der sachliche Anwendungsbereich der DSGVO unverändert bestehen.

answer: I cannot give advice on whether you should appeal a specific fine. However, under the GDPR you have a right to an effective judicial remedy against a legally binding decision of a supervisory authority [2] and also a right to an effective judicial remedy against a controller or processor when your rights have been infringed [9].
